lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: For a minute or two she stood looking at the house, and wondering what to do next, when suddenly a footman in livery came running out of the wood—(she considered him to be a footman because he was in livery: otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish)—and rapped loudly at the door with his knuckles. It was opened by another footman in livery, with a round face, and large eyes like a frog; and both footmen, Alice noticed, had powdered hair that curled all over their heads. She felt very curious to know what it was all about, and crept a little way out of the wood to listen.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Fish-Footman began by producing from under his arm a great letter, nearly as large as himself, and this he handed over to the other, saying, in a solemn tone,

lines.speaker: Frog-Footman
lines.text: “For the Duchess. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Frog-Footman repeated, in the same solemn tone, only changing the order of the words a little,

lines.speaker: Frog-Footman
lines.text: “From the Queen. An invitation for the Duchess to play croquet.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Then they both bowed low, and their curls got entangled together.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice laughed so much at this, that she had to run back into the wood for fear of their hearing her; and when she next peeped out the Fish-Footman was gone, and the other was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up into the sky.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice went timidly up to the door, and knocked.

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “There’s no sort of use in knocking,”

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “and that for two reasons. First, because I’m on the same side of the door as you are; secondly, because they’re making such a noise inside, no one could possibly hear you.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And certainly there was a most extraordinary noise going on within—a constant howling and sneezing, and every now and then a great crash, as if a dish or kettle had been broken to pieces.

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “There might be some sense in your knocking,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the Footman went on without attending to her,

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “if we had the door between us. For instance, if you were inside, you might knock, and I could let you out, you know.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He was looking up into the sky all the time he was speaking, and this Alice thought decidedly uncivil.

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “his eyes are so very nearly at the top of his head. But at any rate he might answer questions.—How am I to get in?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: At this moment the door of the house opened, and a large plate came skimming out, straight at the Footman’s head: it just grazed his nose, and broke to pieces against one of the trees behind him.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the Footman continued in the same tone, exactly as if nothing had happened.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked Alice again, in a louder tone.

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “Are you to get in at all?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was, no doubt: only Alice did not like to be told so.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “the way all the creatures argue. It’s enough to drive one crazy!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Footman seemed to think this a good opportunity for repeating his remark, with variations.

lines.speaker: Footman
lines.text: “on and off, for days and days.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Footman, and began whistling.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Oh, there’s no use in talking to him,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And she opened the door and went in.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The door led right into a large kitchen, which was full of smoke from one end to the other: the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby; the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron which seemed to be full of soup.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “There’s certainly too much pepper in that soup!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice said to herself, as well as she could for sneezing.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: There was certainly too much of it in the air. Even the Duchess sneezed occasionally; and as for the baby, it was sneezing and howling alternately without a moment’s pause. The only things in the kitchen that did not sneeze, were the cook, and a large cat which was sitting on the hearth and grinning from ear to ear.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, a little timidly, for she was not quite sure whether it was good manners for her to speak first,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She said the last word with such sudden violence that Alice quite jumped; but she saw in another moment that it was addressed to the baby, and not to her, so she took courage, and went on again:—

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I didn’t know that Cheshire cats always grinned; in fact, I didn’t know that cats could grin.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I don’t know of any that do,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice said very politely, feeling quite pleased to have got into a conversation.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice did not at all like the tone of this remark, and thought it would be as well to introduce some other subject of conversation. While she was trying to fix on one, the cook took the cauldron of soup off the fire, and at once set to work throwing everything within her reach at the Duchess and the baby—the fire-irons came first; then followed a shower of saucepans, plates, and dishes. The Duchess took no notice of them even when they hit her; and the baby was howling so much already, that it was quite impossible to say whether the blows hurt it or not.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice, jumping up and down in an agony of terror.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: as an unusually large saucepan flew close by it, and very nearly carried it off.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the Duchess said in a hoarse growl,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “the world would go round a deal faster than it does.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, who felt very glad to get an opportunity of showing off a little of her knowledge.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Just think of what work it would make with the day and night! You see the earth takes twenty-four hours to turn round on its axis—”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice glanced rather anxiously at the cook, to see if she meant to take the hint; but the cook was busily stirring the soup, and seemed not to be listening, so she went on again:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Twenty-four hours, I think; or is it twelve? I—”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And with that she began nursing her child again, singing a sort of lullaby to it as she did so, and giving it a violent shake at the end of every line:

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text:
“Speak roughly to your little boy,
And beat him when he sneezes:
He only does it to annoy,
Because he knows it teases.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: CHORUS. (In which the cook and the baby joined):

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: While the Duchess sang the second verse of the song, she kept tossing the baby violently up and down, and the poor little thing howled so, that Alice could hardly hear the words:—

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text:
“I speak severely to my boy,
I beat him when he sneezes;
For he can thoroughly enjoy
The pepper when he pleases!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Here! you may nurse it a bit, if you like!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the Duchess said to Alice, flinging the baby at her as she spoke.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: and she hurried out of the room. The cook threw a frying-pan after her as she went out, but it just missed her.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice caught the baby with some difficulty, as it was a queer-shaped little creature, and held out its arms and legs in all directions,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: thought Alice. The poor little thing was snorting like a steam-engine when she caught it, and kept doubling itself up and straightening itself out again, so that altogether, for the first minute or two, it was as much as she could do to hold it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: As soon as she had made out the proper way of nursing it, (which was to twist it up into a sort of knot, and then keep tight hold of its right ear and left foot, so as to prevent its undoing itself,) she carried it out into the open air.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “If I don’t take this child away with me,”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “they’re sure to kill it in a day or two: wouldn’t it be murder to leave it behind?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She said the last words out loud, and the little thing grunted in reply (it had left off sneezing by this time).

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “that’s not at all a proper way of expressing yourself.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The baby grunted again, and Alice looked very anxiously into its face to see what was the matter with it. There could be no doubt that it had a very turn-up nose, much more like a snout than a real nose; also its eyes were getting extremely small for a baby: altogether Alice did not like the look of the thing at all.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she thought, and looked into its eyes again, to see if there were any tears.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “If you’re going to turn into a pig, my dear,”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I’ll have nothing more to do with you. Mind now!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The poor little thing sobbed again (or grunted, it was impossible to say which), and they went on for some while in silence.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice was just beginning to think to herself,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Now, what am I to do with this creature when I get it home?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: when it grunted again, so violently, that she looked down into its face in some alarm. This time there could be no mistake about it: it was neither more nor less than a pig, and she felt that it would be quite absurd for her to carry it further.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So she set the little creature down, and felt quite relieved to see it trot away quietly into the wood.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “it would have made a dreadfully ugly child: but it makes rather a handsome pig, I think.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And she began thinking over other children she knew, who might do very well as pigs, and was just saying to herself,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “if one only knew the right way to change them—”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: when she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards off.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Cat only grinned when it saw Alice. It looked good-natured, she thought: still it had very long claws and a great many teeth, so she felt that it ought to be treated with respect.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she began, rather timidly, as she did not at all know whether it would like the name: however, it only grinned a little wider.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: thought Alice, and she went on.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Would you tell me, please, which way I ought to go from here?”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “Then it doesn’t matter which way you go,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice felt that this could not be denied, so she tried another question.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “What sort of people live about here?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the Cat said, waving its right paw round,

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “lives a Hatter: and in that direction,”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “lives a March Hare. Visit either you like: they’re both mad.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “But I don’t want to go among mad people,”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice didn’t think that proved it at all; however, she went on

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “And how do you know that you’re mad?”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “a dog’s not mad. You grant that?”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “you see, a dog growls when it’s angry, and wags its tail when it’s pleased. Now I growl when I’m pleased, and wag my tail when I’m angry. Therefore I’m mad.”

lines.speaker: Cat
lines.text: “Do you play croquet with the Queen to-day?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice was not much surprised at this, she was getting so used to queer things happening. While she was looking at the place where it had been, it suddenly appeared again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice quietly said, just as if it had come back in a natural way.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Cat, and vanished again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice waited a little, half expecting to see it again, but it did not appear, and after a minute or two she walked on in the direction in which the March Hare was said to live.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “the March Hare will be much the most interesting, and perhaps as this is May it won’t be raving mad—at least not so mad as it was in March.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: As she said this, she looked up, and there was the Cat again, sitting on a branch of a tree.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and I wish you wouldn’t keep appearing and vanishing so suddenly: you make one quite giddy.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Cat; and this time it vanished quite slowly, beginning with the end of the tail, and ending with the grin, which remained some time after the rest of it had gone.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Well! I’ve often seen a cat without a grin,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “but a grin without a cat! It’s the most curious thing I ever saw in my life!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She had not gone much farther before she came in sight of the house of the March Hare: she thought it must be the right house, because the chimneys were shaped like ears and the roof was thatched with fur. It was so large a house, that she did not like to go nearer till she had nibbled some more of the lefthand bit of mushroom, and raised herself to about two feet high: even then she walked up towards it rather timidly, saying to herself

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Suppose it should be raving mad after all! I almost wish I’d gone to see the Hatter instead!”
